name: Workshop
description: A room for making things, which in a traditional house was not a room at all but a corner of a barn, a cellar or a shed. It reappears in the contemporary programme as a real requirement and has no inherited position, so it has to be placed on first principles: dirty, noisy, wants a wide door and a hard floor, and must not share a wall with a bedroom.

history.note: Domestic making moved out of the house with industrialization and came back as a hobby. The room has no traditional name because the thing it replaced — the barn, the woodshed, the summer kitchen — was outside.

dimensions.critical_dimension: Clear length for material. Sheet goods are 8 ft and lumber comes in 12 and 16, so a 10 ft room cannot rip a sheet without going outside.

furniture.note: Needs 8 ft in front and behind, which is what actually sizes the room.

daylight.orientation: North for even light on a bench

should_adjoin.why: Shares the wide door, the hard floor and the dust tolerance.
Working outside in good weather doubles the room.

must_not_adjoin.why: Noise, and the times of day do not overlap in a good way.
Dust migration and the door that gets left open.

servicing.ventilation: Dust collection and a make-up air path; a sealed shop with a dust collector will depressurize a house and backdraft a flue.
servicing.heat: Independent, because the room is used intermittently
servicing.electrical: 240 V circuit and far more outlets than seems reasonable

style_variation.note: The one style with an ideological claim on this room. Stickley's whole argument assumes a household that makes things, and putting the shop where it can be seen is consistent rather than eccentric.
The connected farmstead already has the right position for it — a link between house and barn.

sources: Hubka, Big House, Little House, Back House, Barn
